blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A population is the complete, explicitly defined set of units about which you want to draw conclusions. A sample is the subset of that population you actually observe. Primary data are data you collect yourself for your question; secondary data were collected by someone else, usually for another purpose (a register, a survey dataset, a programme report), and you reuse them.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Suppose you want the mean haemoglobin of every pregnant woman in Chhattisgarh. Examining all of them is too slow and too expensive, so you examine a manageable subset and use it to infer about the whole. That gap between what you want to know and what you can measure is why inferential statistics exists. A census (every unit measured) removes the need for sampling-based inference, but not for statistics: measurement error, change over time and questions of cause remain.

Whether primary or secondary, data become useful in stages. Data are raw recorded values (each antenatal care (ANC) visit’s haemoglobin). Information is data organised and summarised so that it answers a question (“38% of women seen this quarter had haemoglobin (Hb) below the cut-off”). Intelligence is information interpreted and combined with context so that someone can act on it (“the rise is concentrated in two blocks where iron–folic acid supply broke down; redirect stock there”).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Population: all children under 5 in a district during a given year. Sample: the children who happened to visit one sub-centre this month. This sample may represent the population badly, because children who never visit a facility are excluded by design. Whether a sample represents its population is the subject of Chapter 6.

A resident who weighs 200 children in a village survey collects primary data. A resident who analyses the district’s HMIS reports (§1.4.4) uses secondary data: cheap and large, but the variables, definitions and quality were fixed by someone else.

points.html: Define the population before sampling: “all children under 5 in District X during 2025” is defined; “children” is not.
Numbers computed from a sample estimate the corresponding (usually unknown) population numbers; §1.3 names them.
A census is the case where the sample equals the population. It is rare because of cost, though national censuses are done (§1.4.4).
Secondary data: check who collected them, for what purpose, with which definitions and denominators, and how complete they are, before analysing them.
